title: Coffee eclairs
subtitle: choux pastry fingers filled with coffee creme patissiere and topped with coffee fondant
excerpt: Coffee eclairs are choux pastry fingers filled with a coffee creme patissiere and finished with a coffee-flavoured fondant or icing. The choux is piped into batons and baked until hollow and golden, then the base is pierced and the filling piped in. The fondant sets into a smooth, glossy top. Eclairs are best eaten on the day they are assembled.
sourceNotes: The eclair is a French pastry first documented in the nineteenth century, the name possibly derived from the French word for lightning, though the etymology is uncertain. Coffee and chocolate are the two classic flavours. The recipe appears in Mrs Beeton and in French patisserie manuals throughout the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cooked pastry dough made by heating water, butter, and flour together then beating in eggs. It puffs into a hollow shell during baking due to the steam trapped inside.
A thick, cooked egg and milk custard used as a pastry filling. It sets firm enough to pipe but stays smooth and creamy.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unfilled, cooled eclairs on a flat tray for up to 1 month. Defrost at room temperature and refresh in a 160 degrees C oven for 5 minutes before filling.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The creme patissiere can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. Assemble on the day of serving.

content.text: and finished with a coffee glaze. The choux must be baked long enough to fully dry out inside; underbaked eclairs collapse as they cool. The filling goes in through a small hole in the base or end, piped until the shell feels heavy.

items.prepNote: dissolved in 1 tbsp hot water, for creme patissiere and glaze

content.text: Make the creme patissiere first: bring the milk to a gentle simmer. Whisk the yolks, sugar, and cornflour together until smooth. Pour the hot milk into the yolk mixture in a slow stream, whisking constantly. Return to the pan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until the cream is thick and bubbling, about 3 to 4 minutes. Remove from the heat, stir in 1 teaspoon of the dissolved espresso. Press cling film directly onto the surface and refrigerate until cold.

Make the choux: bring the water and butter to the boil in a medium saucepan. Remove from the heat and tip in all the flour at once. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon until the mixture leaves the sides of the pan and forms a smooth ball. Cook out on the heat for 1 minute, stirring.

Leave the dough to cool for 5 minutes so the eggs do not scramble. Add the beaten eggs a little at a time, beating well between each addition. The paste is ready when it is smooth, glossy, and drops slowly from the spoon when lifted and shaken; you may not need all the egg.

Heat the oven to 200 degrees C (fan 180 degrees C / gas 6). Line two baking trays with baking paper. Transfer the choux to a piping bag with a 1.5 cm plain nozzle. Pipe batons about 12 cm long, spaced well apart. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until deep golden and feeling hollow and light when lifted. Do not open the oven in the first 20 minutes. Make a small hole in each end immediately out of the oven to let steam escape. Cool on a rack.

Beat the cold creme patissiere until smooth. Transfer to a piping bag with a small plain nozzle. Push the nozzle into the hole at one end of each eclair and pipe until you feel the shell fill up and become heavy.

Make the glaze: sift the icing sugar into a bowl and stir in the remaining dissolved espresso and enough water (1 to 2 tablespoons) to make a smooth, pourable icing. Dip the top of each filled eclair into the glaze, letting the excess drip back. Place on a rack for 20 minutes for the glaze to set.

attrs.problem: Eclairs collapsing inward as they cool
attrs.avoid: Avoid underbaking; collapsed eclairs mean the inside was not fully dry when they left the oven.
attrs.fix: Bake until deeply golden and feeling light. Pierce a hole in each end immediately out of the oven to release steam. If they are still collapsing, reduce the oven temperature by 10 degrees and extend the baking time.

attrs.problem: Choux paste too stiff and dry, not dropping from the spoon
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding all the beaten egg at once; you may need less or more than the recipe states.
attrs.fix: Add the egg a tablespoon at a time, beating fully after each addition. Stop when the paste drops slowly from the spoon in a thick, smooth ribbon.
